B makes the studio name the hero, sets it in a large serif with a terracotta italic ampersand, keeps the one-liner short and shows all three cards in full, so it fits the request more closely. A's 'Shape something real' headline has strong personality, but it pushes the name into the small nav and runs the 'one line' to three lines. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both pages use a system serif for display and a system sans for reading, with the same warm terracotta-and-cream palette, and neither appears to load external assets. A follows the brief more closely: the studio name is the large hero headline, followed by a true one-line description, and all three cards fit cleanly in view. B's italic 'real' adds some personality, but it makes a tagline the headline, shrinks the name into the nav, uses a longer paragraph instead of one line, and its cards are cut off at the bottom of the screenshot.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both pages pair a serif display face with a sans for body text, use a warm clay and sage palette, and give each element a clearly different weight. A has more personality: its serif feels more deliberate, the italic clay ampersand and green 'Fern' stand out, and the left-aligned layout with soft blurred shapes feels more modern. B's centered Georgia-style headline is clean but closer to the default look, though its card body text is a bit easier to read than A's light, small gray text. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both pages pair a system serif display face with a system sans for reading, use the same warm palette and follow the same card structure. B's type has more character (a refined old-style serif plus a geometric sans like Avenir), and its left-aligned, asymmetric layout feels more modern than A's centered Georgia-and-Helvetica layout, which looks more like a template. B's light-gray card body text is a little thinner and harder to read than A's, but B is still the stronger overall design.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both use a two-family system: a serif for display and card titles, and a system sans for reading text and buttons. Both also show clear hierarchy and a warm palette, with no script or novelty faces. B's serif headline, which looks like Iowan Old Style, has more character than A's Georgia-like face, and its two-tone name, small wordmark nav and eyebrow rule make the layout feel more deliberate and modern. The screenshots can't confirm that neither file loads external assets, but both appear to render in system fonts. The bottom of B's cards is cut off in the screenshot. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use the same sound approach: a system serif for the name and card titles, a system sans for the reading text and button, and a warm terracotta-and-cream palette with no external assets. A's display serif feels more refined and distinctive than B's Georgia-like face, and the two-tone 'Kiln & Fern' plus the small header strengthen the hierarchy. B fits more neatly in the viewport, but its type has a little less personality.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B picks Georgia, which ships on Mac, Windows and iOS, and says plainly what Android falls back to. It also catches that Georgia's old-style numerals are a problem on invoices, and gives specific checks for metric differences across platforms. A leads with Iowan Old Style, which only Mac and iOS have, so most Windows users see Palatino instead. A's reasons for the pairing are thinner, and it calls licensing moot instead of naming what to upgrade to once licensing is cleared. B doesn't do that either: its only upgrade suggestion is other system fonts. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): A picks Georgia, which looks much the same on Mac, Windows and iOS, and pairs it with the system sans. It also explains why the pairing suits law firms and flags a real billing pitfall: Georgia's old-style numerals make invoice amounts hard to scan. B's lead face, Iowan Old Style, exists only on Mac and iOS, so Windows and Android users will see a different heading font, and B dismisses licensing as moot without saying what to upgrade later. Neither answer clearly lays out a web-font upgrade for when legal clears licenses.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B gives a clear Georgia plus system-sans pairing with full fallback stacks. It explains in plain terms why the pair reads as established and is easy to scan, and it is explicit that text will look different on each platform, with concrete overflow checks for Windows and Android. A's Palatino-first stack is valid and splits product UI from marketing sensibly, but its reasoning is thin ('heritage, measured tone'). Neither answer says what to upgrade once licensing clears, and B wrongly suggests Palatino is missing on Windows without Office. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers name concrete stacks of system fonts, with fallbacks and tabular figures for billing amounts. A explains the choice more clearly: Georgia was built for screens, and the system sans is what each OS already uses for dense UI. A also gives more practical checks, such as Segoe and Roboto being wider than SF and causing overflow in invoice tables. B's split between product UI and marketing site is sensible, but its reasoning ('heritage, measured tone') is thinner, and neither answer says what to upgrade to once legal clears the licenses.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick Georgia for headings and the system-UI sans for body, with sound cross-platform stacks. B makes a strong point about Georgia's old-style numerals in billing contexts and clearly states that no font looks identical across platforms. A wins narrowly because it also gives an upgrade path once licensing clears, adds practical guidance on Georgia's limited weights and font-synthesis, and covers Android more directly with Noto Serif. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers pick Georgia for headings and the system sans for body, with good cross-platform stacks and practical warnings: A covers Georgia's old-style numerals and Mac-only faces, and B covers Georgia's limited weights and font-synthesis. B wins because it says what to upgrade once licensing clears and explains the pairing a little more clearly. A never addresses the post-licensing upgrade.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers catch the core problems: too many fonts, Montserrat and Poppins looking nearly alike, and Courier New on the phone numbers. B goes further for older readers by recommending Atkinson Hyperlegible, asking for clearly different I/l/1 and O/0, and giving a real system fallback stack. B has a small inconsistency, saying 'five different families' and then listing six, and its claim that Poppins makes I, l and 1 look alike is debatable. A is accurate and concise, and its point that heading levels switch between serif and sans is a sharp, CSS-specific catch. B's broader readability advice and fallback handling still make it the better answer overall. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly say that too many overlapping families cause the messy look, and both point out the Montserrat/Poppins near-duplicate and the Courier New phone number. A does more for older patients: it asks for clear I/l/1 and O/0 letterforms, recommends Atkinson Hyperlegible and adds tabular figures. It also gives a real system fallback stack, though it says 'five' families before listing six. B's best catch is the serif/sans switch at each heading level (h1 to h3), but it has a confusing 'five style categories' claim, and its only fallback is a bare 'sans-serif'.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): B's diagnosis is a bit sharper: it points out the h1 serif / h2 sans / h3 serif swaps and adds body size and line-height to its CSS. But B's replacement CSS leaves out .phone-number from the font rule, so the phone number stays in Courier New, the issue B itself calls the biggest. B also wrongly says Courier has uneven digit widths, though it is a monospace font with equal-width digits. A's fix is complete, gives a real system font fallback list, and names clear jobs for each font. A's one slip is suggesting Lora for h1 and h3, which brings back some of the serif/sans switching. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain that too many overlapping families cause the messy look and recommend cutting down to Open Sans, with Lora as an optional heading serif. B is stronger on practical details: it gives a real system fallback stack, recommends 18px+ body text with more line spacing, and suggests tel: links. A says Courier New has 'uneven digit widths', which is wrong because Courier is monospaced. B has its own flaw: putting Lora on h1 and h3 but not h2 brings back the alternating heading styles it should be removing.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B better explains the messy feeling: it names the overlapping roles, with two near-identical geometric sans faces, two serifs with no clear job, and a third sans for body text. It also gives a cleaner system-font fallback stack. A is stronger for older patients, with an 18px body size and 1.6 line height, while B has a contradictory point 5 ('Light weights' described as 'heavy and wide') and an unnecessary licensing note. Both reduce the set to a single family and use tabular-nums for phone numbers, so B wins only narrowly. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A explains the overlapping roles more clearly, pointing out the two near-identical geometric sans faces and the two serifs with no clear jobs. However, its fifth point is titled 'Light weights for headings' and then describes heavy, wide faces, which contradicts itself. Answer B fits older patients better, with 18px body text, more line height, and a direct case for making phone numbers readable, and it also notes the fallback risk if the Google Fonts link is missing, so it is slightly better overall.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B says plainly that the setup is ready to ship, but two of its points are wrong. Descendant cells of .tide-table inherit font-variant-numeric anyway, and font-feature-settings can't help a font that lacks tabular figures. It also suggests swapping in Roboto or Inter as a web font. A runs long and is phrased as changes rather than optional tweaks, but its advice is accurate and low-risk, and it never suggests replacing the families. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A opens by saying the setup is ready to ship, which is what a quick check should do, but two of its points are wrong. Cells inside .tide-table already inherit font-variant-numeric, and a font-feature-settings fallback can't help a font that lacks tabular figures. It also suggests a web font (Inter). Answer B's advice is more accurate and useful, including the .meta tabular-nums nuance and the missing bold and italic faces, but it frames the CSS as 'things I'd change' and adds line-height, max-width and size changes, so it reads closer to a redesign than a sanity check.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers say plainly that the setup is sound and that nothing blocks shipping. A has a small factual error: on Windows the stack would reach Sitka Text before Cambria. A also floats bundling a web font, which comes close to suggesting new families, though only conditionally. B gives the more useful practical fixes (right-aligning the numeric columns, matching sans and serif sizes) and correctly lists Sitka. However, B adds some padding: the monospace and naming items, and it overstates how much tabular-nums depends on right-alignment. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers say the setup is sound and avoid lists of trendy fonts. A gives a concrete reason it works (system stacks with no web-font load flash) and keeps its suggestions small, with the right-alignment fix as the main practical one. B suggests bundling a web-font sans and makes that its key point, which edges toward replacing the families. Its faux-bold point is also mostly padding.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B says plainly that the setup is sound. It names concrete strengths, such as tabular-nums for aligned tide times and generic fallbacks with no web-font loading, and keeps its checks few, accurate and clearly marked as optional. A also says the setup is solid but never explains what works. Its five tweaks read more like a punch list, and some are misdirected: the old-style numeral point is about serif figures, but the tide table uses the sans stack, and the claim about missing bold on Linux is shaky. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Answer A says plainly that the setup is sound, explains concretely why it works (separate roles, real generic fallbacks, tabular-nums for the tide table), and limits itself to two checks plus one optional cleanup that is clearly labeled. Answer B also calls the setup solid, but it lists five suggestions and some of them are off. The lining-nums advice assumes a serif face, yet the tide table uses the sans stack. The claim that system-ui on Linux may have no true bold is shaky. Together these make B read more like a list of changes than a quick check.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain variable fonts clearly, avoid overselling them, and say honestly that the licence can't be known from the file name. B wins because it states the desktop-versus-web licence split more directly, adds a check on whether the designer has the right to pass the font on, and offers to help read the licence. A uses a few undefined terms, such as "@font-face" and "x-height". Neither mentions system fonts or which file format to use for the web. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain variable fonts accurately, avoid overselling them, are honest that they can't tell the licence from the file, and separate desktop licences from web licences. A suits a non-technical bakery owner better: it defines 'axes' in plain words and adds a useful point about whether the designer actually has the rights to pass on. B gives more concrete terms to search for in the licence, but it leaves jargon undefined (x-height, @font-face, embedding, and 'axis' before it's explained). Neither answer mentions system fonts or which file format to use on the web.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain variable fonts clearly, say they are not automatically better, and warn that a desktop licence may not cover web use. A says outright that the .ttf file alone can't show what the licence allows, and its Font Book tip is easy for a non-technical owner to follow. B gives more practical steps: it mentions the .woff2 web format, warns that some licences forbid converting the file, and suggests getting permission in writing. Each answer's strengths balance out. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain variable fonts clearly, say a normal font is just as good when only a couple of styles are needed, and point out that a desktop licence often differs from web use. A gives more practical steps, including the .woff2 format, checking whether conversion is allowed and getting permission in writing, though it slightly overstates that .ttf is only for desktop use. B states more directly that the .ttf file alone can't show the licence and mentions visitor or pageview limits, but it says nothing about web file formats.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers explain variable fonts clearly and handle the licence question honestly, including the difference between desktop and web licences. A wins narrowly on practical next steps: it shows how to check the licence on a Mac, gives clear questions to ask the designer, and names the web format to request (WOFF2). B is more balanced on when separate static files are smaller and offers Google Fonts as a backup, but it leaves terms like 'EULA' and 'embedding' unexplained and doesn't mention web file formats. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers explain variable fonts clearly, avoid overselling them, and are honest that the file alone cannot show whether web use is allowed. B gives more practical next steps: it names the web format to ask for (.woff2), shows how to check font info in Font Book, gives two ready-to-send questions, and defines terms like licence and foundry. A has good advice, including a sample message and a Google Fonts fallback, but leaves 'EULA' undefined and never mentions a web font format.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=without, B=with): Both answers recommend a coordinated Noto setup with separate faces per script, lang and dir tagging, bidi isolation for Latin stop names, and taller line-height per script. A covers more ground but drifts into line breaking, dark mode, truncation and pseudo-locale testing. It also contains doubtful claims: that Noto Sans Arabic's Latin glyphs match Noto Sans, and that word-break: auto-phrase works in Safari 17+. B stays closer to the typeface decisions, adds tabular figures for the departure times, and admits it hasn't checked licensing or file sizes, though it has a stray font-synthesis declaration outside any CSS rule. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers pick per-script Noto faces with language-tagged stacks. B is more complete: it covers size-adjust, per-language line height, digit choice, bidi isolation, and the platform trade-off between bundled and system Japanese fonts (Hiragino, Noto CJK), and its testing plan is stronger. A is more focused but thinner on platform gaps and has a stray `font-synthesis` declaration outside any rule. B overstates that Noto Sans Arabic's Latin glyphs match Noto Sans, and it strays into line breaking, truncation and dark mode, which costs it on focus.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B gives each script its own stack with named platform fallbacks (Geeza Pro, Hiragino Sans, Yu Gothic) and is clear about what needs testing on real devices. It also handles Latin stop names inside Arabic and Japanese cleanly and stays on typeface choices. A is detailed and mostly accurate, but it drifts into layout and accessibility advice (row budgets, WCAG contrast), and it says little about platform fallbacks beyond recommending that fonts be bundled. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): Both answers give each script its own face, use lang attributes and bdi isolation for Latin stop names, and flag line-height and size differences. A pairs each script with named system fallbacks (Geeza Pro, Hiragino Sans, Yu Gothic), stays on typeface decisions, and admits what it hasn't verified. B covers more script-specific detail and device testing, but its stack has no system fallbacks, it includes some shaky advice like full-width spacing around Latin names, and it drifts into general layout, contrast and repo commentary.

pass 1 (A=without, B=with): B is the better answer, mainly because it handles embedded Latin stop names more convincingly. It puts the Latin face first in each script's stack and uses one designed-together family (Noto), so stop names inside Arabic and Japanese match in weight and size. It is also more open about what it hasn't verified and about platform fallbacks, and stays closer to typeface decisions. A is technically rich, with metric overrides and a per-script `lang` setup, but drifts into general RTL layout, icon mirroring and severity design. | pass 2 (A=with, B=without): A picks one coordinated family (Noto) for all three scripts and puts the Latin face first in each stack. That directly answers the question of making embedded Latin stop names match the surrounding weight and size. A also hedges honestly about licensing and coverage, and says to test with the fonts blocked. B covers more script-specific detail, such as Arabic letter-spacing, Han glyph variants and line-break rules, but it mixes Inter with other script faces without saying how to match their weights. It also drifts into general bidi, icon-mirroring and alert-hierarchy layout advice, and gives less clear guidance on system-font gaps.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly identify proportional figures as the cause, give a `tabular-nums` fix to paste, and keep Gill Sans. Answer A says more about checking for the `tnum` feature and names Calibri as a concrete fallback, but its point about platform metrics is a distraction. Answer B applies the fix to exactly the price and seat columns and explains more accurately how right alignment and commas interact, so it is slightly tighter and more on target. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers correctly blame proportional figures and give a working tabular-nums fix that keeps Gill Sans. B is more thorough on rubric item 4: it shows how to check for the tnum feature, notes that the macOS and Windows versions of Gill Sans differ, and gives a concrete fallback. A explains more precisely why the commas don't break right alignment. B's claim that Calibri's default figures are tabular is plausible but not verified.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly blame proportional figures and give a working `tabular-nums` fix while keeping Gill Sans. B is stronger on the fallback case: it admits it can't check the installed font, explains how to check for `tnum`, and offers a numerals-only `@font-face` with `unicode-range`. It also notes that the Calibri fallback may explain why the problem shows up on some machines and not others. A's `min-width: 6ch` fallback does not actually fix uneven digit widths, which makes that part of its advice inaccurate. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers correctly blame proportional figures and give the same tabular-nums CSS for the price and seat cells, while keeping Gill Sans. A handles missing font support better: it explains how to check for tnum and suggests a numerals-only @font-face with unicode-range. B's min-width in ch units fallback would not fix uneven digit widths. B does a little better at explaining why right alignment and comma placement still matter.

pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both answers correctly identify proportional figures as the cause and give a pasteable tabular-nums fix that keeps Gill Sans. B is stronger: it keeps right alignment in the fix, adds lining-nums to handle old-style figures, and honestly says CSS cannot fake tabular figures when the font lacks them. A's fallback, a min-width inline-block span, would not actually align digits of different widths, and its DevTools check confirms the property is set rather than that the font supports it, a flaw B shares. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers correctly identify proportional figures as the cause and keep Gill Sans. B's fallback is wrong: a fixed-width inline-block span with min-width in ch only pads the whole number, so the digits inside are still proportional and won't line up. A is right that CSS can't fake tabular figures. A's DevTools check is weak because the Computed panel shows the declared value, not whether the font supports tnum, but that is a smaller flaw than B's.

samples.judge_notes: pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pages use a cream, paper-like serif-and-mono design that avoids the usual dark-mode template, and both separate track from artist well. B has the stronger title, and its playlist is easier to read at a glance: artists are set in small uppercase roman and track titles in italic. A sets artists in small caps and titles in roman, so the two lines are closer in weight and parse less quickly. B's tuning-dial ruler adds an analog touch without leaning on gradients, but its card runs past the bottom of the screenshot, while A's compact layout fits in full. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both answers use a similar warm paper card with a serif title, a monospace label face and side-labeled tracklists, and neither looks like a generic dark-mode page. A edges ahead: its large italic title has more presence, the uppercase artist over italic track separates each line clearly, and the tuning-dial ruler adds an analog touch through drawing rather than effects. pass 1 (A=with, B=without): Both pages use a serif with a mono on a warm paper ground, and neither looks like a generic dark-mode template. B leans more on decoration (rotated paper, tape, a bevelled gradient button), though its serif-title versus mono-caps-artist split makes the playlist slightly easier to read. | pass 2 (A=without, B=with): Both pages pair a literary serif with a monospace on a cream ground and avoid the usual dark-mode template. B gets its mood more from type alone: an italic title over small-caps 'Radio', a log-style playlist with timestamps, and a flat button set in the page's mono.
